title: Number Bases and the Binary System
summary: What a number base is, how decimal and binary place values work, and why computers use binary.

p: A number base (or radix) is the number of different digits, including zero, that a counting system uses. In base 10 (the decimal system we use every day) there are ten digits: 0 to 9. Each place stands for a power of 10. For example, 345₁₀ = 3 × 10² + 4 × 10¹ + 5 × 10⁰ = 300 + 40 + 5.

Base 2 (binary) uses only 0 and 1, and each place is a power of 2. Example: 101₂ = 1 × 2² + 0 × 2¹ + 1 × 2⁰ = 4 + 0 + 1 = 5₁₀. Base 8 (octal) uses the digits 0 to 7. Base 16 (hexadecimal) uses 0 to 9 and the letters A to F for ten to fifteen. The small number written low and to the right of a numeral, the subscript, tells us the base.

A computer is built from millions of tiny electronic switches. A switch can be ON or OFF, and that matches exactly two digits: ON = 1 and OFF = 0. This is simple, reliable and fast, and it is the foundation of all digital technology. Each binary digit is called a bit (short for 'binary digit'). Eight bits make one byte.
Study the table. Each place is double the one on its right.
In decimal, ten ones make one ten and we write 10. In binary, two ones make one 'two' and we write 10₂. So 2₁₀ = 10₂, and 10₂ is read 'one-zero', not 'ten'.

title: Converting Between Binary and Decimal
summary: Two methods of changing binary to decimal and decimal to binary, with fully worked examples and answers to the exercises.

p: Multiply each binary digit by its place value and add. Example 1: 101₂ = 1×4 + 0×2 + 1×1 = 5. Example 2: 1101₂ = 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13. Example 3: 10110₂ = 16 + 0 + 4 + 2 + 0 = 22. Example 4: 11111₂ = 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 31. Example 5: 100101₂ = 32 + 0 + 0 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 37.

sections.h: Decimal to binary: repeated division by 2
p: 1. Divide the number by 2. 2. Write down the remainder (0 or 1). 3. Divide the quotient by 2 again. 4. Keep going until the quotient is 0. 5. Read the remainders from the bottom up.
Example 6: 13₁₀. 13 ÷ 2 = 6 remainder 1; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 remainder 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 remainder 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 remainder 1. Reading upward: 1101₂.
Find the largest power of 2 that fits, subtract it and write 1 in that place; write 0 for each place you skip; repeat with what is left.

Example 9: 26₁₀. 26 is less than 32, so start at 16: 26 – 16 = 10 (1 in the 16's place); 10 – 8 = 2 (1 in the 8's place); 4's place is skipped (0); 2 – 2 = 0 (1 in the 2's place); 1's place is 0. So 26₁₀ = 11010₂.
Example 10: 45₁₀ = 32 + 8 + 4 + 1, so the places 32, 8, 4 and 1 hold a 1 and 16 and 2 hold a 0: 101101₂.
Evaluation: 1011₂ = 11; 19₁₀ = 10011₂; 10101₂ = 21; 32₁₀ = 100000₂; 4 bits can show 2⁴ = 16 values.
Always convert back. 75 = 64 + 8 + 2 + 1, so its binary is 1001011, and 64 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 75 confirms it.

title: Binary Counting, Bits, Bytes and Computers
summary: Counting in binary from 0 to 20, how many values n bits can store, and how computers store numbers in bytes.

p: Study the table.
Each time you use one more binary digit, the number of values you can show doubles. 1 bit shows 2 values, 2 bits show 4, 3 bits show 8, and so on. n bits show 2ⁿ values, from 0 up to 2ⁿ – 1.

1 bit is the smallest unit, 0 or 1. 1 byte = 8 bits and can show 0 to 255. Computer memory is usually counted in 1 kilobyte (KB) = 1,024 bytes, 1 megabyte (MB) = 1,024 KB and 1 gigabyte (GB) = 1,024 MB. (Some makers use 1,000 instead of 1,024 in advertisements, so a flash drive may show a little less space than its label.)

Example 11: 3 bits give 2³ = 8 values, from 000₂ to 111₂ (0 to 7). Example 12: 8 bits give 2⁸ = 256 values, from 00000000₂ to 11111111₂ (0 to 255). Example 13: the number 10 is 1010₂, and in an 8-bit byte it is stored as 00001010. Example 14: 01100100₂ = 64 + 32 + 4 = 100.

Values by number of bits: 2 bits = 4; 5 bits = 32; 6 bits = 64. Largest number: 4 bits = 15; 7 bits = 127; 8 bits = 255. 8-bit forms: 15 = 00001111; 50 = 00110010; 128 = 10000000. Decimal values: 00010101 = 21; 01100100 = 100; 11110000 = 240.

sections.h: Simple expressions (let the number be x)
p: The sum of a number and 5: x + 5. Three times a number: 3x. Five less than a number: x – 5 (not 5 – x: the order matters). The product of a number and 8: 8x. A number divided by 4: x ÷ 4 or x/4. Twice a number increased by 7: 2x + 7. The difference between a number and 10: x – 10. Half of a number decreased by 3: x/2 – 3.
'5 less than x' means start with x and take away 5: x – 5. 'x less than 5' means start with 5 and take away x: 5 – x. Read the sentence from the number being reduced.

The sum of a number and 9: x + 9. A number decreased by 7: x – 7. Five times a number: 5x. A number divided by 6: x/6. Eight more than a number: x + 8. Ten less than a number: x – 10. The product of a number and 12: 12x. Half of a number: x/2. Twice a number increased by 5: 2x + 5. Three times a number decreased by 4: 3x – 4. The quotient of a number and 5: x/5. Six less than four times a number: 4x – 6. The sum of a number and twice the number: x + 2x = 3x. Half a number plus 8: x/2 + 8. A number squared minus 10: x² – 10.
Evaluation: 'a number increased by 12': x + 12; 'four less than twice a number': 2x – 4.

title: Translating Words into Equations and Solving Word Problems
summary: How to turn a story into an equation, solve it, and check it, with a seven-step method and worked problems on numbers, ages, money and perimeter.

p: 1. Read carefully and understand the question. 2. Find the unknown. 3. Let x stand for it. 4. Find the relationships (more than, less than, times). 5. Write the equation. 6. Solve it. 7. Check that the answer makes sense.
Example 23: 'A number increased by 8 equals 20': x + 8 = 20, so x = 12.
Example 24: 'Five times a number is 35': 5x = 35, so x = 7.
Example 25: 'The sum of a number and twice the number equals 24': x + 2x = 24, so 3x = 24 and x = 8.
Example 26: three consecutive numbers add to 36: x + (x + 1) + (x + 2) = 36, so 3x + 3 = 36, 3x = 33 and x = 11. The numbers are 11, 12 and 13.
Example 27: John is 5 more than twice Mary's age and is 23: 2x + 5 = 23, so 2x = 18 and Mary is 9.
Example 28: a rectangle's length is 3 cm more than its width and the perimeter is 26 cm: 2(w + 3 + w) = 26, so 2(2w + 3) = 26, 2w + 3 = 13 and w = 5. The width is 5 cm and the length is 8 cm.

Example 29: a father is 4 times as old as his son; in 5 years he will be 3 times as old. Let the son be x now: 4x + 5 = 3(x + 5), so 4x + 5 = 3x + 15 and x = 10. The son is 10 and the father is 40. Check: in 5 years they are 15 and 45, and 45 = 3 × 15.
Example 30: a shopkeeper sells at a 25% profit for ₦50. Cost price x: 1.25x = 50, so x = ₦40.
Example 31: Peter has ₦500 more than James and together they have ₦2,000. James x: x + (x + 500) = 2,000, so 2x = 1,500 and x = 750. James has ₦750 and Peter ₦1,250.
Example 32: pencils cost ₦50 each, pens ₦80 each; 5 pencils and some pens cost ₦650: 250 + 80p = 650, so 80p = 400 and p = 5 pens.

A number increased by 15 equals 40: x + 15 = 40. Three times a number is 27: 3x = 27. A number divided by 4 equals 8: x/4 = 8. Five less than a number is 12: x – 5 = 12. Twice a number plus 7 equals 25: 2x + 7 = 25. A number divided by 3, then increased by 5, equals 11: x/3 + 5 = 11. The product of a number and 6, decreased by 8, is 40: 6x – 8 = 40. Half of a number plus the number itself is 21: x/2 + x = 21.
A man's age is twice his son's; ten years ago he was 3 times as old. Son x now: father 2x. Ten years ago: 2x – 10 = 3(x – 10), so x = 20 (son 20, father 40).
The sum of two numbers is 50 and one is 8 more than the other: x + (x + 8) = 50, so x = 21 and the numbers are 21 and 29.

title: Direct Proportion
summary: What it means for two quantities to be directly proportional, the unitary and proportion methods, the constant of proportionality, and uses in money, distance, maps and recipes.

p: Two quantities are in direct proportion if they go up or down together at the same rate: when one doubles, so does the other. We write y ∝ x, which means y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality. Also y ÷ x is always the same, so y₁/x₁ = y₂/x₂.
Example 19: 5 books cost ₦1,000; find the cost of 8 books. Unitary method: 1 book = 1,000 ÷ 5 = ₦200, so 8 books = 8 × 200 = ₦1,600. Proportion method: 5/1,000 = 8/x gives 5x = 8,000 and x = ₦1,600.
Example 21: 3 m of cloth cost ₦450. Cost of 7 m: 3x = 450 × 7 = 3,150, so x = ₦1,050.
Example 22: a car travels 240 km in 3 hours; in 5 hours at the same speed it travels 240 ÷ 3 × 5 = 400 km.
Example 23: y is directly proportional to x and y = 12 when x = 4. (a) y = kx, so 12 = 4k and k = 3. (b) y = 3x, so when x = 7, y = 21.

title: Inverse Proportion
summary: Quantities that change in opposite directions, the product rule x₁y₁ = x₂y₂, and examples with workers, speed and time.

p: Two quantities are inversely proportional when one increases as the other decreases, at the same rate: when one doubles, the other halves. We write y ∝ 1/x, so y = k/x and x × y is always the same: x₁y₁ = x₂y₂.
Example 24: 6 workers finish a job in 8 days. How long for 12 workers? Workers × days is constant: 6 × 8 = 12 × d, so 48 = 12d and d = 4 days. Check: more workers, less time.
Example 25: at 60 km/h a journey takes 4 hours. At 80 km/h: 60 × 4 = 80t, so t = 3 hours.
Example 26: y is inversely proportional to x and y = 6 when x = 5. (a) k = xy = 30. (b) y = 30 ÷ x, so when x = 10, y = 3.

Example 27: 20 men dig a trench in 15 days. For 10 days: 20 × 15 = m × 10, so m = 30 men. (The workers example that the note first put in direct proportion, 12 workers in 5 days, needs 60 ÷ 3 = 20 workers for 3 days.)

sections.h: How to decide between direct and inverse
p: Ask: if one quantity doubles, what happens to the other? If it also doubles: direct. If it halves: inverse. More workers, less time (inverse). More books, more cost (direct). Higher speed, less time for the same trip (inverse).

title: Compound Interest and Depreciation
summary: How interest on interest grows money, the formula A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ, half-yearly and quarterly compounding, finding principal and rate, and depreciation.

p: Compound interest is worked out on the principal plus the interest already earned in earlier periods. The formula is A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ, where A is the final amount, P the principal (starting money), r the rate per period in percent and n the number of periods. Compound interest = A – P.
Compare with simple interest I = PRT/100, which is worked out on the principal only. Simple interest grows in a straight line; compound interest grows faster, like a snowball.

Example 31: ₦10,000 at 5% a year for 2 years. A = 10,000 × (1.05)² = 10,000 × 1.1025 = ₦11,025. CI = 11,025 – 10,000 = ₦1,025. Simple interest would be 10,000 × 5 × 2 ÷ 100 = ₦1,000, so compound interest is ₦25 more.
Example 33: what principal grows to ₦15,000 at 10% for 2 years? 15,000 = P × 1.21, so P = 15,000 ÷ 1.21 = ₦12,396.69.
Example 34: at what rate does ₦20,000 become ₦24,200 in 2 years? 24,200 ÷ 20,000 = 1.21 = (1 + r)², so 1 + r = 1.1 and r = 10%.

sections.h: Compounding more than once a year
p: Divide the yearly rate by the number of periods in a year and multiply the number of years by the same number.
Example 35: ₦30,000 at 12% a year compounded half-yearly for 1 year: rate 6% per half-year, 2 periods. A = 30,000 × 1.06² = 30,000 × 1.1236 = ₦33,708. CI = ₦3,708.
Example 36: ₦40,000 at 8% compounded quarterly for 1 year: 2% per quarter, 4 quarters. A = 40,000 × 1.02⁴ = 40,000 × 1.08243216 = ₦43,297.29. CI = ₦3,297.29.
Depreciation is a loss of value each period. Use A = P(1 – r/100)ⁿ. Example 37: a car worth ₦2,000,000 depreciates 15% a year. After 3 years: 2,000,000 × 0.85³ = 2,000,000 × 0.614125 = ₦1,228,250.
Evaluation: CI on ₦5,000 at 10% for 2 years: 5,000 × 1.21 = 6,050, so CI = ₦1,050.
